title: Government orders legal review of Stelco steel plant in Ottawa
summary: The Attorney General's office has asked for a full review of the lease and environmental permits held by the Stelco steel works in east Freetown.
bodyHtml:
The Attorney General's office has requested a legal review of the Stelco steel plant in the Ottawa industrial area of east Freetown, according to a letter circulated to ministries this week.

The review covers the plant's lease, its environmental permits and the terms under which scrap metal is imported and processed at the site.

What the review covers

Officials describe the exercise as administrative. It is intended to establish whether the permits held by the company match the scale of operations now running at the plant.

If the permits do not match what is happening on the ground, then the law already tells us what to do next, a ministry official said.

Residents of Ottawa and Calaba Town have complained for two years about dust, night-time noise and heavy truck traffic on the main access road.

The company has not commented publicly. The Ministry of Trade says normal operations continue while the review is under way, and Parliament's trade committee is expected to ask for the findings when sittings resume.
author: Mohamed Konneh
imageCaption: The Stelco steel works on the eastern edge of Freetown.

title: Parliament committee backs changes to mining royalty sharing
summary: A parliamentary committee has approved amendments that would raise the share of mining revenue paid to chiefdoms and district councils.
bodyHtml:
The Mines and Minerals Committee has approved a set of amendments that would change how royalty payments from large mining operations are shared with the districts that host them.

Under the proposal, a larger share of the surface rent and the royalty would be paid directly to chiefdom administrations rather than passing through the consolidated fund.

Where the money goes

Supporters argue that direct payments would make it easier for communities in Kono, Koinadugu and Bonthe to see what their districts receive.

Communities have been told for years that the money is coming. If they can see the figure, they can ask the right question, the committee chair said.

Officials at the Ministry of Finance have warned that ring-fencing revenue reduces the flexibility needed to fund national programmes, and have asked for a phased start.

The amendments now return to the floor of Parliament for a second reading, where the finance committee is expected to propose a three-year transition.
author: Isatu Bangura
imageCaption: A parliamentary committee session at Tower Hill.

title: Freetown City Council rolls out ward-level waste collection
summary: The council has contracted 14 local groups to collect household waste ward by ward, starting in the east of the city.
bodyHtml:
Freetown City Council has begun a ward-by-ward waste collection programme, contracting 14 community groups to run daily pickups in the eastern districts before extending west.

Each group is responsible for a defined set of streets and reports to a council supervisor, a change from the single citywide contract the council previously relied on.

Why the change

Council officials say smaller contracts are easier to monitor and let them pay collectors weekly rather than at the end of a long contract cycle.

Households will pay a monthly fee, with a reduced rate for registered compounds that share a single bin. Enforcement begins with warnings rather than fines.

Traders at the King Jimmy and Sani Abacha markets have asked for extra collections on market days, when volumes roughly double.

The council expects the programme to cover all wards by the end of the first quarter and says it will publish monthly collection figures.
author: Abu Bakarr Sesay
imageCaption: Waste collection crews working in central Freetown.

title: Diamond exports rise as official channels take a bigger share
summary: Third-quarter exports rose by value as more of the country's alluvial production moved through the national export authority.
bodyHtml:
Diamond exports rose in value in the third quarter, according to figures released by the National Minerals Agency, as a larger share of alluvial production passed through official valuation.

Volumes were broadly flat, which means the increase came from a better mix of stones rather than from more digging.

Why official channels are growing

Dealers credit the opening of additional valuation points in Kono and Kenema and a shorter wait for export certificates.

Artisanal miners still sell most of their production locally to licensed dealers, who then decide whether to export or hold stock.

The agency says a pilot programme that records the identity of each digger at the point of sale will be extended to two more chiefdoms next quarter.

Analysts caution that a single quarter is not a trend, and that smuggling remains a persistent problem on the eastern border.
author: Fatmata Kargbo
imageCaption: Sorting and valuation of alluvial diamonds in Kono.

title: Bank of Sierra Leone holds policy rate as inflation cools
summary: The central bank kept its policy rate unchanged, saying food prices had eased but the leone still faced pressure from import costs.
bodyHtml:
The Bank of Sierra Leone left its policy rate unchanged at its latest monetary policy meeting, citing slower food price growth and a stable exchange rate over the past two months.

Headline inflation has fallen for three consecutive readings, though it remains well above the level the bank considers comfortable.

What the bank said

The monetary policy committee noted that rice and fuel imports continue to set the floor for household costs, and that a poor harvest in the north would keep pressure on prices into the first quarter.

Lending rates at commercial banks have not moved in step with the policy rate, and the committee repeated its call for faster transmission.

Private sector groups welcomed the decision to hold, saying an increase would have raised borrowing costs for businesses still recovering from last year's slow season.

The next meeting is scheduled for December, when the committee will also publish its revised growth forecast.
author: Samuel Bangura
imageCaption: The Bank of Sierra Leone headquarters on Siaka Stevens Street.

title: Koidu licence review puts small-scale buyers under scrutiny
summary: Authorities in Kono district have begun verifying the licences of dealers who buy from artisanal diamond and gold diggers.
bodyHtml:
A verification exercise has begun in Koidu targeting the dealers and buying agents who purchase from artisanal diamond and gold diggers across Kono district.

Teams from the district mining office are checking dealer licences, purchase records and the receipts that diggers are supposed to receive for every sale.

Why dealers are being checked

Officials say the aim is to close the gap between what is declared at export and what is actually dug, a gap that has widened as prices for larger stones improved.

Diggers interviewed in Tankoro said they supported the checks but wanted the receipt system to work in practice, not only on paper.

Two dealers had their trading certificates suspended pending the production of records covering the past six months.

The exercise is expected to run for four weeks, after which the district office will publish a list of verified buyers.
author: Sorie Kamara
imageCaption: A mining office record check in Koidu, Kono district.

title: Rutile and bauxite output recovers after a slow start to the year
summary: Shipments from the south-west resumed at near-normal volumes after haul-road repairs, the mines ministry said.
bodyHtml:
Rutile and bauxite shipments from the south-west have returned to near-normal volumes after repairs to the haul road that links the mines to the storage sites.

Output had fallen sharply in the first quarter when heavy rain cut the road in two places and forced trucks onto a longer route.

The cost of the detour

The ministry estimates the detour added roughly a third to haulage costs during the affected months, a burden the operators absorbed rather than passing on.

Two culverts have been rebuilt and a section of the road has been raised above the flood line, work the ministry says should hold through the coming rainy season.

Community groups along the route have again asked for dust suppression and for a share of the road maintenance budget.

The ministry expects full-year volumes to be close to last year's, with a stronger final quarter.
author: Alhaji Turay
imageCaption: Haul trucks on the mineral road in the south-west.

title: Malaria vaccine reaches a third of eligible under-twos
summary: Health teams have delivered the first two doses to about 120,000 children since the rollout began, with Bo and Kenema leading coverage.
bodyHtml:
About 120,000 children under two have received their first two doses of the malaria vaccine since the national rollout began, according to the expanded programme on immunisation.

Coverage is highest in Bo and Kenema districts, where teams combined vaccination rounds with existing child health clinics.

Where coverage lags

Remote chiefdoms in Koinadugu and Falaba remain the hardest to reach, particularly where roads become impassable in the rains.

Health workers say the main constraint is not hesitancy but the cold chain, which requires reliable power at the last storage point before a village session.

Two districts have begun using solar-powered vaccine carriers, an approach the programme will evaluate before deciding whether to scale it up.

The vaccine is given alongside existing malaria prevention, and officials stress that bed nets and prompt testing remain the first line of defence.
author: Dr Aminata Jalloh
imageCaption: A child health clinic during a vaccination round.

title: Guma Valley announces 12-hour shutdown for western Freetown
summary: Supply will be cut on Saturday from 6am while a transmission main between Regent and Wilberforce is repaired.
bodyHtml:
Guma Valley Water Company has announced a 12-hour shutdown of supply to western Freetown on Saturday, beginning at 6am, while crews repair a transmission main between Regent and Wilberforce.

The company says the main has leaked twice in the past month and that the repair has been scheduled for a weekend to limit the effect on schools and offices.

Which areas are affected

Supply will be interrupted in Wilberforce, Regent, Gloucester, Leicester and parts of Hill Station, with lower pressure expected as far as Congo Cross.

We know the timing is inconvenient. The alternative is a failure in the middle of the week, when hospitals and schools need water most, a company engineer said.

Tankers will be stationed at four points in the affected districts, and the company has asked hospitals to draw from their reserves during the day.

Normal supply is expected to resume by early evening, though airlocks in the higher streets may take several hours to clear.
author: Mariama Sankoh
imageCaption: A Guma Valley repair crew working on a transmission main.

title: Teacher training colleges add a second intake to close staffing gaps
summary: Four colleges will run an extra intake next year as districts report unfilled posts in primary science and mathematics.
bodyHtml:
Four teacher training colleges will run a second intake next year to help districts fill vacant primary posts, particularly in science and mathematics.

The additional intake adds roughly 1,100 places, most of them reserved for candidates who agree to teach in the district where they trained.

Why the gaps persist

District education offices report that many trained teachers decline rural postings, and that replacements often take a full term to arrive.

The Teaching Service Commission says it will publish posting lists earlier this year so that schools know who is coming before the term begins.

Colleges have also revised the practical component of the certificate, doubling the time student teachers spend in classrooms under supervision.

Lecturers warn that the extra intake will strain hostel space, and two colleges are negotiating to use nearby secondary school dormitories.
author: Josephine Williams
imageCaption: Student teachers during a supervised classroom session.

title: ECOWAS ministers agree a timetable for a standby force review
summary: Regional ministers set a March deadline for proposals on funding and troop contributions for the ECOWAS standby force.
bodyHtml:
Regional ministers have agreed a March deadline for proposals on how the ECOWAS standby force should be funded and how troop contributions should be shared among member states.

The decision followed two days of talks in Abuja that focused on the logistics depot at Lungi and on the force's ability to deploy without a lengthy funding round.

The funding question

Officials acknowledge that the force has been declared ready faster than it has been financed, and that several pledged units have not yet reached full equipment levels.

A separate working group will examine whether the community levy can cover a standing readiness budget rather than case-by-case deployments.

Ministers also discussed cooperation with the African Union on intelligence sharing and on the movement of equipment across borders.

A progress report is expected at the next summit, with a first joint exercise planned for the second half of the year.
author: BBC Africa
imageCaption: Delegates at the regional ministerial meeting.

title: Record cocoa prices reshape West African export earnings
summary: Producers in the region are renegotiating supply contracts after global prices held near historic highs for a second season.
bodyHtml:
Cocoa prices have held close to historic highs for a second season, changing the arithmetic for West African exporters and for the farmers who supply them.

Several producer countries have raised the fixed farmgate price they pay growers, aiming to capture part of the gain before the next harvest.

The risk of holding back

Some cooperatives have delayed sales in the expectation of further gains, a strategy that carries real risk if prices fall sharply.

Buyers, meanwhile, are signing longer contracts to secure volume, particularly for certified and traceable beans that attract a premium.

Analysts warn that high prices encourage planting elsewhere, and that a supply response in Latin America and Asia could soften the market within three years.

For now, the bigger constraint in the region is not demand but ageing trees and the cost of replacing them.
author: BBC Africa
imageCaption: Cocoa beans drying ahead of sale.

title: Leone Stars level with Guinea as AFCON qualifier goes to the wire
summary: Sierra Leone equalised early in the second half at the National Stadium and need a win to keep qualification in their own hands.
bodyHtml:
Sierra Leone equalised early in the second half of the AFCON qualifier against Guinea at the National Stadium, setting up a tense final twenty minutes in Freetown.

Guinea took the lead against the run of play, finishing a counter-attack after a Sierra Leone corner was cleared to the halfway line.

How the equaliser came

The Leone Stars levelled from a low cross that was turned in at the near post, sending the home sections of the stadium into noise that could be heard across Murray Town.

Sierra Leone have since pushed a second striker forward, leaving space behind the full-backs that Guinea have twice failed to exploit.

The crowd is carrying us now. We have twenty minutes to win a football match, the captain shouted to the bench before the restart.

A win would put qualification in Sierra Leone's own hands with one round of fixtures remaining, while a draw leaves the group to be decided on the final matchday.

Follow this page for updates as the closing stages unfold.
author: Sahr Morris Jr
imageCaption: The Leone Stars in action at the National Stadium in Freetown.

title: Bo Rangers edge Mighty Blackpool to stay top of the Premier League
summary: A late header at the Southern Arena kept Bo Rangers two points clear with the second half of the season approaching.
bodyHtml:
Bo Rangers beat Mighty Blackpool 2-1 at the Southern Arena to stay top of the Sierra Leone Premier League, with a late header settling a match that had looked destined for a draw.

Blackpool had taken the lead in the first half from a free kick, before Rangers levelled shortly after the interval through a deflected shot from the edge of the area.

The table after the weekend

The win keeps Rangers two points clear of East End Lions, who play Kamboi Eagles at the Trade Centre next weekend in the pick of the fixtures.

Mighty Blackpool stay third, and their coach said afterwards that the team had lost concentration at the one moment it could not afford to.

Kamboi Eagles, in fourth, have a game in hand and could close to within a point of the leaders if they win it.

The league returns after a short break for the national team's qualifying fixtures.
author: Mohamed Fajah
imageCaption: Bo Rangers celebrate the winning goal at the Southern Arena.

title: Freetown's lantern parade returns with 40 competing groups
summary: Organisers expect the biggest parade in a decade as groups from the east end finish weeks of costume building.
bodyHtml:
Forty groups have registered for this year's lantern parade in central Freetown, the largest field organisers can remember in a decade.

The parade follows its traditional route through the east end before finishing at the National Stadium, where judging takes place after dark.

Months of preparation

Groups begin building in August, working from compounds in Wellington, Calaba Town and Kissy on structures that can be carried through the streets.

This year's entries include a lantern depicting the Bo-Kenema highway and another shaped like a fishing boat, a nod to the communities along the peninsula.

Organisers have asked the council for additional lighting along the route and for traffic to be diverted from the early evening.

Prizes are awarded for craft, choreography and the size of the accompanying drumming section, which judges say is often what decides the closest contests.
author: Zainab Conteh
imageCaption: A lantern group preparing for the parade in east Freetown.

title: ECOFEST adds Salone artists to a three-night Freetown lineup
summary: Organisers say the festival will run three nights at the National Stadium with a stage reserved for Sierra Leonean acts.
bodyHtml:
ECOFEST will run for three nights at the National Stadium, with one stage reserved entirely for Sierra Leonean artists alongside the visiting headline acts.

The festival has grown steadily since its first edition, and organisers say ticketing will again be split between physical outlets and mobile money.

A stage for local acts

The decision to reserve a stage follows criticism that earlier editions gave local performers short sets at the start of the evening.

Artists on the bill include established names and a handful of acts who built audiences on social media over the past two years.

Sound checks will run across two days, and organisers have promised a published set timetable before the gates open.

Hotels in the Aberdeen and Lumley areas report strong bookings for the weekend, with several already full.
author: Kadijatu Bah
imageCaption: Crowds at a previous ECOFEST night in Freetown.

title: Mobile money interoperability cuts transfer times across networks
summary: Transfers between the three largest mobile money wallets now settle in minutes, the payments switch said.
bodyHtml:
Transfers between the three largest mobile money wallets now settle in minutes rather than hours, according to the national payments switch.

The change follows a reconnection of the interoperability platform to the settlement accounts used by each provider.

What changes for users

Customers no longer need to move cash out of one wallet and into another to pay a merchant on a different network.

Merchants say the biggest practical gain is at the end of the day, when reconciliation used to require matching two sets of records.

Fees remain the same for now, though the switch has asked providers to publish a common schedule so customers can compare.

Fintech developers have asked for sandbox access to the interoperability interface so that smaller services can build on it.
author: Ibrahim Koroma
imageCaption: A mobile money agent serving customers in Freetown.

title: Vehicle imports climb as the Bo-Kenema highway nears completion
summary: Dealers at the Queen Elizabeth II Quay report a rise in used-vehicle imports, with buyers counting on the new road.
bodyHtml:
Dealers at the Queen Elizabeth II Quay report a rise in used-vehicle imports this quarter, with buyers citing the near-complete Bo-Kenema highway as a reason to buy.

The route has been the most difficult long-distance drive in the country for years, and dealers say customers in the south-east are now willing to buy vehicles they would previously have avoided.

What buyers are choosing

Small saloons still dominate, but demand for light pickups has grown sharply among traders who move goods between Bo and Kenema.

Importers say customs clearance times have improved slightly, though the cost of shipping and the exchange rate still set the final price.

Mechanics in Bo have asked for training on the electronic systems used in newer models, arguing that servicing capacity will otherwise lag the vehicles arriving.

The road is due to open fully before the next rainy season, subject to the completion of two bridges.
author: Bockarie Mansaray
imageCaption: Vehicles awaiting clearance at the Queen Elizabeth II Quay.

title: New vehicle inspection centre opens in Kissy
summary: Drivers in the east end of Freetown can now complete roadworthiness checks at a new inspection bay, the transport authority says.
bodyHtml:
The transport authority has opened a vehicle inspection centre in Kissy, adding capacity to a system that has struggled with long queues at the central Freetown depot.

The centre will handle private cars, taxis and light commercial vehicles. Officials say the first phase will operate six days a week while additional testing lanes are commissioned.

What drivers need

Drivers should bring their vehicle registration, current insurance and the previous inspection certificate where available. The fee schedule is unchanged.

Transport unions welcomed the extra capacity but asked for clearer public notice of the opening hours and for a separate lane for commercial passenger vehicles.
author: Aminata Sesay
imageCaption: Vehicles waiting for inspection in Freetown.

title: Used-car imports slow as new levies take effect
summary: Dealers at the Freetown port report fewer vehicle clearances this month as buyers adjust to the revised import charges.
bodyHtml:
Used-car imports through the Queen Elizabeth II Quay have slowed as dealers and buyers adjust to revised clearing charges introduced this month.

Several dealers said buyers are waiting to see how the new schedule is applied before committing to orders. The customs authority says the changes are intended to make valuations more predictable.

Buyers cautious

A dealer at the port said smaller petrol cars remain the most requested, while demand for larger vehicles has weakened. Buyers are also asking more often for pre-purchase inspections.

Port officials expect clearance volumes to settle once the first full billing cycle is completed.
author: Mohamed Kamara
imageCaption: Vehicles at the Freetown port.

title: Krio gospel choir announces national tour
summary: The choir will take its Krio-language repertoire to Bo, Kenema and Makeni before a closing concert in Freetown.
bodyHtml:
A Freetown Krio gospel choir has announced a national tour, with performances planned in Bo, Kenema and Makeni before a closing concert in the capital.

The programme mixes traditional hymns with new arrangements written for the tour. Organisers say the Bo and Kenema shows will feature local youth choirs as opening acts.

Local stages

Rehearsals are being held at a community hall in the east end, and the choir is raising money for transport and sound equipment through ticket sales.

Ticket prices were kept low for students, and a portion of the proceeds will go to a school music programme.
author: Fatmata Koroma
imageCaption: Choir rehearsal in Freetown.

title: Local music platform starts paying artists per stream
summary: A Sierra Leonean streaming service says it will publish monthly payout statements for artists on its platform.
bodyHtml:
A Sierra Leonean music streaming platform has begun paying artists per stream and says it will publish monthly payout statements for participating musicians.

The company says the move is intended to make revenue sharing more transparent for artists who mostly distribute through social media and messaging apps.

Building a catalogue

The platform is signing local labels and independent artists, including several Krio and Temne-language acts. Artists will retain ownership of their recordings, according to the terms.

Industry workers welcomed the payout model but said payment thresholds and reporting need to be clear enough for small acts to participate.
author: Ibrahim Conteh
imageCaption: A recording session in Freetown.

title: National museum reopens textile gallery
summary: The gallery has been closed for refurbishment and now displays country cloth and woven textile pieces from across Sierra Leone.
bodyHtml:
The national museum has reopened its textile gallery after a refurbishment, putting country cloth and woven pieces from several regions back on public display.

The collection includes examples of local weaving, natural dyeing and ceremonial cloth. Curators say they are also recording the stories of the weavers and families who donated pieces.

A living collection

The museum plans to host weaving demonstrations and school visits during the opening season, and is asking families with historical pieces to contact its collections team.

Entry remains free for school groups, and the gallery has added labels in English and Krio.
author: Mariama Turay
imageCaption: Textile display at the national museum.

title: Bo cultural festival brings together dance and crafts
summary: The two-day festival will feature dance groups, craft sellers and oral history sessions in the centre of Bo.
bodyHtml:
A two-day cultural festival in Bo will bring together dance groups, craft sellers and oral history sessions in the city centre.

The programme includes performances from community groups across the south and a market for locally made goods. Organisers say they want younger residents involved in planning the next edition.

Local participation

Workshops on cloth dyeing, basket weaving and traditional music are planned alongside the main stage. Food stalls will be run by local traders.

Entry is free, and the organisers have held discussions with the city council about traffic and waste management.
author: Abdul Rahman Jalloh
imageCaption: Craft sellers at a cultural festival.
